{{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. [[file:Kumano-hongû-taisha Shrine - Torii at Ôyunohara.jpg|alt=Largest Torii in the world|left|thumb|Otorii]] In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == [[file:Kumano-hongû-taisha Shrine - Shaden.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha main temple]] Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]
Haiden (Worship Hall) | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Hongu, Tanabe|ja|本宮町本宮}} 1100 | coordinates = {{Coord|33|50|24.9|N|135|46|24.9|E|display=inline,title}} | deities = {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神}} | shrine_Rank = {{ubl|{{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|1=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|fr|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社}})|Former {{ill|Kanpei-taisha|ja|官幣大社}}|{{ill|Bekkaku shrine|ja|別表神社}}}} | founded = Traditionally attributed to the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇}}'s reign | pilgrimage = {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|神仏霊場巡拝の道}} (4th station in Wakayama) | festival = April 15 ([[Kumano Hongu Taisha Grand Festival|御田祭]]) | main_building = {{ubl|{{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} (First and Second Halls)|{{ill|Kirizuma-zukuri|ja|切妻造}} (front) and {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} (rear) (Third and Fourth Halls)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Wakayama|lat_deg=33|lat_min=50|lat_sec=27.1|lon_deg=135|lon_min=46|lon_sec=27.4|label=Kumano Hongu Taisha|position=left|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|50|27.1|N|135|46|27.4|E}}}} }} '''Kumano Hongu Taisha''' ({{ill|Kumano Hongu Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, ''Kumano Hongū Taisha'') is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. Alongside {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|ja|熊野速玉大社}} and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社}}, it forms the {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|ja|スサノオ}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! Hall !! name !! deity !! Honji Buddha |- | First Hall || West Front Hall || {{ill|Kumano Musubi Ōkami|ja|熊野牟須美大神}}, {{ill|Kumano Gongen|lt=Koto-sakarai|ja|事解之男神}} || {{ill|Senju Kannon|ja|千手観音}} |- | Second Hall || Central Front Hall || {{ill|Hayatama-no-Mikoto|ja|速玉之男神}} || {{ill|Yakushi Nyorai|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha}} |- | Third Hall || Main Hall || {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神}} || {{ill|Amida Nyorai|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |- | Fourth Hall || East Front Hall || {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami}} || {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|lt=Jūichimen Kannon|ja|十一面観音}} |} The halls, dating to the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代}}, are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties.{{Cite web|url=http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/|title=国指定文化財等データベース|publisher=文化庁}} == Cultural Significance == === Yatagarasu === {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏}}, a three-legged crow, is a symbol of guidance and the shrine's divine messenger. |publisher=熊野本宮大社|url=http://www.hongutaisha.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%92%AB%E7%83%8F/|accessdate=2020-03-23}} === UNESCO World Heritage === Kumano Hongu Taisha is part of the {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|12=draft}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|12=draft}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|12=draft}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|12=draft}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|12=draft}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|12=draft}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|ja|スサノオ|12=draft}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|12=draft}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|12=draft}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|12=draft}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|12=draft}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|12=draft}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|12=draft}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|12=draft}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社|12=draft}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|12=draft}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|12=draft}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|12=draft}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! {{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]

In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]

Alongside {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|ja|熊野速玉大社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社|qq=draft}}, it forms the {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|qq=draft}}. The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|ja|スサノオ|qq=draft}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|qq=draft}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=draft}}. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|qq=draft}}, were not rebuilt. {{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]
Haiden (Worship Hall) | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Hongu, Tanabe|ja|本宮町本宮|qq=draft}} 1100 | coordinates = {{Coord|33|50|24.9|N|135|46|24.9|E|display=inline,title}} | deities = {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} | shrine_Rank = {{ubl|{{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|1=Shikinaisha|2=ja|3=式内社|qq=draft|1=Shikinaisha|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|fr|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qq=draft}})|Former {{ill|Kanpei-taisha|ja|官幣大社|qq=draft}}|{{ill|Bekkaku shrine|ja|別表神社|1=Beppyo Shrine|2=ja|3=別表神社|4=simple|5=Beppyo shrine|6=zh|7=別表神社|8=mr|9=बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|qq=draft}}}} | founded = Traditionally attributed to the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft}}'s reign | pilgrimage = {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|神仏霊場巡拝の道|qq=draft}} (4th station in Wakayama) | festival = April 15 ([[Kumano Hongu Taisha Grand Festival|御田祭]]) | main_building = {{ubl|{{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造|qq=draft}} (First and Second Halls)|{{ill|Kirizuma-zukuri|ja|切妻造|qq=draft}} (front) and {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造|qq=draft}} (rear) (Third and Fourth Halls)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Wakayama|lat_deg=33|lat_min=50|lat_sec=27.1|lon_deg=135|lon_min=46|lon_sec=27.4|label=Kumano Hongu Taisha|position=left|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|50|27.1|N|135|46|27.4|E}}}} }} '''Kumano Hongu Taisha''' ({{ill|Kumano Hongu Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社|qq=draft}}, ''Kumano Hongū Taisha'') is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft}} located in {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県|qq=draft}}, Japan. Alongside {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|ja|熊野速玉大社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社|qq=draft}}, it forms the {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|qq=draft}}. The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|ja|スサノオ|qq=draft}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|qq=draft}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=draft}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社|qq=draft}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|qq=draft}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! Hall !! name !! deity !! Alongside {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|ja|熊野速玉大社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社|qq=draft}}, it forms the {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|qq=draft}}. The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|ja|スサノオ|qq=draft}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|qq=draft}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=draft}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社|qq=draft}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|qq=draft}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! It is believed to have led {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇|qq=draft}} to the Yamato region, symbolizing wisdom and divine intervention.{{Cite news|title=八咫烏について |publisher=熊野本宮大社|url=http://www.hongutaisha.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%92%AB%E7%83%8F/|accessdate=2020-03-23}} === UNESCO World Heritage === Kumano Hongu Taisha is part of the {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft}}, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. == Access == * '''Bus:''' From {{ill|JR Shingu Station|ja|新宮駅|qq=draft}}, 1 hour via Kumano Kotsu buses. * '''Car:''' Parking available. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.hongutaisha.jp/ Official Website of Kumano Hongu Taisha] * [https://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/bcms/sekaiisan/index.html Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes (Wakayama Prefecture)] == References == {{reflist}} == External links == {{commons-inline}} * [http://sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/sisan/sanzan.html Wakayama World Heritage Center] * [http://hongutaisha.jp Kumano Hongū Taisha Official Site] (Japanese) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20070827102007/www2.ocn.ne.jp/~sanzan/NTTcontents/hongu Kumano Sanzan Official Site] (Japanese) {{shinto shrine}}{{Kumano Faith}} {{citation needed|Kumano Hongu Taisha}} ]] {{Kujūku Ōji|bottom}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{translated page|ja|熊野本宮大社|version=104192163|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:Kumano Sanzan| ]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Taisha]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Expanded pages from Wikipedia]] [[Category:Kumano Hongū Taisha]] [[Category:Kujūku Ōji]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] }} [[file:Kumano-hongû-taisha Shrine - {{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. {{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]
Haiden (Worship Hall) | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Hongu, Tanabe|ja|本宮町本宮|qq=draft}} 1100 | coordinates = {{Coord|33|50|24.9|N|135|46|24.9|E|display=inline,title}} | deities = {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} | shrine_Rank = {{ubl|{{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|1=Shikinaisha|2=ja|3=式内社|qq=draft|1=Shikinaisha|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|fr|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qq=draft}})|Former {{ill|Kanpei-taisha|ja|官幣大社|qq=draft}}|{{ill|Bekkaku shrine|ja|別表神社|1=Beppyo Shrine|2=ja|3=別表神社|4=simple|5=Beppyo shrine|6=zh|7=別表神社|8=mr|9=बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|qq=draft}}}} | founded = Traditionally attributed to the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft}}'s reign | pilgrimage = {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|神仏霊場巡拝の道|qq=draft}} (4th station in Wakayama) | festival = April 15 ([[Kumano Hongu Taisha Grand Festival|御田祭]]) | main_building = {{ubl|{{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造|qq=draft}} (First and Second Halls)|{{ill|Kirizuma-zukuri|ja|切妻造|qq=draft}} (front) and {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造|qq=draft}} (rear) (Third and Fourth Halls)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Wakayama|lat_deg=33|lat_min=50|lat_sec=27.1|lon_deg=135|lon_min=46|lon_sec=27.4|label=Kumano Hongu Taisha|position=left|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|50|27.1|N|135|46|27.4|E}}}} }} '''Kumano Hongu Taisha''' ({{ill|Kumano Hongu Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社|qq=draft}}, ''Kumano Hongū Taisha'') is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft}} located in {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県|qq=draft}}, Japan. Alongside {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|ja|熊野速玉大社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社|qq=draft}}, it forms the {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|qq=draft}}. The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|スサノオ|qq=draft}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|qq=draft}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=draft}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社|qq=draft}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|qq=draft}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! Hall !! name !! deity !! Honji Buddha |- | First Hall || West Front Hall || {{ill|Kumano Musubi Ōkami|ja|熊野牟須美大神|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kumano Gongen|lt=Koto-sakarai|ja|事解之男神|qq=draft}} || {{ill|Senju Kannon|ja|千手観音|qq=draft}} |- | Second Hall || Central Front Hall || {{ill|Hayatama-no-Mikoto|ja|速玉之男神|qq=draft}} || {{ill|Yakushi Nyorai|ja|薬師如来|1=Bhaisajyaguru|lt=Yakushi Nyorai (Me)dicine Buddha|qq=draft}} |- | Third Hall || Main Hall || {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft}} || {{ill|Amida Nyorai|ja|阿弥陀如来|qq=draft}} |- | Fourth Hall || East Front Hall || {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft}} || {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|lt=Jūichimen Kannon|ja|十一面観音|qq=draft}} |} The halls, dating to the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft}}, are nationally designated Important Cultural Properties.{{Cite web|url=http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/|title=国指定文化財等データベース|publisher=文化庁}} == Cultural Significance == === Yatagarasu === {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft}}, a three-legged crow, is a symbol of guidance and the shrine's divine messenger. It is believed to have led {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇|qq=draft}} to the Yamato region, symbolizing wisdom and divine intervention.{{Cite news|title=八咫烏について |publisher=熊野本宮大社|url=http://www.hongutaisha.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%92%AB%E7%83%8F/|accessdate=2020-03-23}} === UNESCO World Heritage === Kumano Hongu Taisha is part of the {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft}}, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. == Access == * '''Bus:''' From {{ill|JR Shingu Station|ja|新宮駅|qq=draft}}, 1 hour via Kumano Kotsu buses. * '''Car:''' Parking available. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.hongutaisha.jp/ Official Website of Kumano Hongu Taisha] * [https://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/bcms/sekaiisan/index.html Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes (Wakayama Prefecture)] == References == {{reflist}} == External links == {{commons-inline}} * [http://sekaiisan-wakayama.jp/english/sisan/sanzan.html Wakayama World Heritage Center] * [http://hongutaisha.jp Kumano Hongū Taisha Official Site] (Japanese) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20070827102007/www2.ocn.ne.jp/~sanzan/NTTcontents/hongu Kumano Sanzan Official Site] (Japanese) {{shinto shrine}}{{Kumano Faith}} ]] {{Kujūku Ōji|bottom}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{translated page|ja|熊野本宮大社|version=104192163|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:Kumano Sanzan| ]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Taisha]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Expanded pages from Wikipedia]] [[Category:Kumano Hongū Taisha]] [[Category:Kujūku Ōji]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] }} [[file:Kumano-hongû-taisha Shrine - The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|qq=}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|スサノオ|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Susanoo|13=User:Immanuelle/Susanoo-no-Mikoto|qq=}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatagarasu|qq=}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izanami|qq=}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kukurihime|qq=}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima|qq=}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heian period|qq=}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Toba|qq=}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano River|qq=}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-sha|qq=}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naka-sha|qq=}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimo-sha|qq=}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyunohara|qq=}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! {{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]

{{short description|Shinto shrine in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{infobox religious building | name = {{nihongo|Kumano Hongū Taisha|熊野本宮大社}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = Shrine Kumano hongu torii01.jpg | caption = Shrine Gate (Torii) of Kumano Hongu Taisha with flag representing [[Yatagarasu]] | map_type = Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|50|24|N|135|46|26|E|display=title,inline|source:dewiki}} | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | deity = Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現) | location = 1110 Hongucho Hongu, [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]] 647-1731, Japan }} {{nihongo|'''Kumano Hongū Taisha'''|熊野本宮大社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the jurisdiction of [[Tanabe, Wakayama]], deep in the rugged mountains of the southeast [[Kii Peninsula]] of [[Japan]]. It is included as part of the [[Kumano Sanzan]] in the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]". The main deity enshrined is Kumano [[Gongen]] (熊野権現). All of the ancient [[Kumano Kodō]] routes lead to the Grand Shrine. It was originally located at present {{Nihongo|Ōyunohara|大斎原}}, on a sandbank at the [[confluence]] of the [[Kumano River]] and Otonashi River. In 1889, it was partially destroyed in a flood and the remaining shrine buildings were relocated at its present site in 1891. Of the original five main pavilions only three were rebuilt. Four deities were moved there and the other eight are still enshrined there in two stone monuments. In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]

Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Hongu Taisha|qq=}}, ''Kumano Hongū Taisha'') is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto shrine|qq=}} located in {{ill|Tanabe|ja|田辺市|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tanabe|qq=}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakayama Prefecture|qq=}}, Japan. Alongside {{ill|Kumano Hayatama Taisha|ja|熊野速玉大社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Hayatama Taisha|qq=}} and {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Nachi Taisha|qq=}}, it forms the {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|qq=}}. The shrine enshrines {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|qq=}} as its primary deity and is a key location in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, {{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|ja|紀伊山地の霊場と参詣道|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|qq=}}. == History == [[File:Kumano-hongû-taisha_Shrine_-_Stone_monument_of_a_crow_"Yatagarasu".jpg|thumb|200px|right|Statue of {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatagarasu|qq=}} at Kumano Hongu Taisha]] The exact date of the shrine's foundation is unknown, but according to legend, it was established in the 65th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Sujin|qq=}}'s reign (traditionally 2nd century CE) on a sandbank in the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano River|qq=}}, now known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyunohara|qq=}}. The shrine has been associated with numerous deities and traditions over time. {{ill|Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|ja|家都美御子大神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ketsumi-miko Ōkami|qq=}}, often identified with {{ill|Susanoo|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|スサノオ|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Susanoo|13=User:Immanuelle/Susanoo-no-Mikoto|qq=}}, has unclear origins. Interpretations of the deity vary, ranging from a solar god (due to the association with {{ill|Yatagarasu|ja|八咫烏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatagarasu|qq=}}, the three-legged crow), a water god (reflecting the shrine's riverside location), to a tree deity. Other theories connect the deity to {{ill|Izanami|ja|イザナミ|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izanami|qq=}}, {{ill|Kukurihime|ja|菊理媛|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kukurihime|qq=}}, or {{ill|Itsukushima|ja|五十猛神|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima|qq=}}.{{Cite book|author=川口謙二|title=日本の神様読み解き事典|year=1999|publisher=柏書房|isbn=978-4-7601-1824-3}} In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heian period|qq=}}, Kumano Hongu Taisha became a major pilgrimage site, attracting emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Toba|ja|鳥羽天皇|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Toba|qq=}} and {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Go-Shirakawa|qq=}}. By the 12th century, the shrine was one of Japan's most significant religious centers. === Flood and Relocation === In 1889, the {{ill|Kumano River|ja|熊野川|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano River|qq=}} flooded, devastating the shrine. Only the {{ill|Kami-sha|ja|上四社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-sha|qq=}} (First to Fourth Halls) survived and were relocated to the current site. The remaining structures, including the {{ill|Naka-sha|ja|中四社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naka-sha|qq=}} and {{ill|Shimo-sha|ja|下四社|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimo-sha|qq=}}, were not rebuilt. Today, two stone altars at {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyunohara|qq=}} commemorate the lost shrines. == Deities and Structure == The shrine consists of four main halls, each enshrining different deities: {| class="wikitable" |+ '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Deities and Buddhas''' ! In 2000, the largest [[torii]] shrine gate in the world (33.9 meters tall and 42 meters wide) was erected at the entrance to the Oyunohara sandbank. It is an official gateway that designates the entrance to a sacred area. It signifies the division of the secular and the spiritual worlds. This torii is called ''Otorii'' (''o'' means "great") and is made of steel weighing 172 tons, which took about six months to make and another six months to assemble.{{Cite web|url = http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/world-heritage/kumano-hongu-taisha/|title = Kumano Hongu Taisha 熊野本宮大社|date = |accessdate = October 9, 2014|website = Sacred Kumano|publisher = Tanabe City Kumona Tourism Bureau|last = |first = }} == History == Over 900 years ago a pilgrim wrote of a massive shrine grounds including five main pavilions enshrining 12 deities. Numerous other small temples and shrines could be found surrounding the main buildings. Over the centuries the pavilions were partially destroyed by periodic fires and flooding, but always faithfully rebuilt to their original state. The last fire was in 1776 and the buildings rebuilt again in 1803. The first drawing of the shrine grounds from over 800 years ago and the reconstruction that took place in 1803 are almost exactly identical. After the flood of 1889, the shrine pavilions were moved and rebuilt at their present location. == Architecture == The Kumano Hongu Taisha's pavilions are an outstanding example of Japanese shrine architecture. The use of natural unfinished materials allows it to blend effortlessly into the natural environment. Intricate joint works were used in the construction instead of nails. The thick roof gracefully sweeps forward extending over the stairs and the area in front of the shrine. It is made entirely of hinoki, Japanese cypress bark. [[File:Kumano Hongu Taisha's roof architecture.jpg|thumb|Hongu Taisha rooftop]] The bronze ornaments on the roof top are characteristic features of shrine architecture. The X-shaped crosspieces that pierce the sky are called Chigi and the log like beams that are laid horizontally along and perpendicular to the ridge line are called Katsuogi. They add a dramatic highlight to the roof line. Unique to the Kumano Hongu Taisha is the space or corridor under the verandas of the pavilions. In the past, the pilgrims and ascetics would use this tiny refuge for meditation, prayer, [[sutra]] copying, austere rites and even sleeping quarters. In fact, this is where Saint [[Ippen|Ippen Shonin]] was enlightened. The Kumano Hongu Taisha is a mixture between Kasuga and Taisha styles but because of this sacred corridor it has also been referred to as the Kumano style. == Festivals == '''Kumano Hongu Taisha Spring Festival''', the annual spring festival held 13–15 April every year, is not only a quintessential festival of Kumano but also intimately associated with the pilgrimage to Kumano and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route. On April 13 fathers and their young sons purify themselves in the [[sacred waters]] of Yunomine Onsen before walking over the Dainichi-goe section of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route to Oyunohara wearing traditional costumes. The young boys have the character for big on their forehead and are forbidden to touch the ground. On April 15 the Kumano Deities are invoked to temporarily take up residence in a portable mikoshi shrine and return to their original site of descend, Oyunohara. The atmosphere is serene, traditional, authentic and inspiring. '''Yata-no-Hi Matsuri Fire Festival''' takes place on the last Saturday of August, in Oyunohara (Hongu-cho), in honour of [[Yatagarasu]]. This fire festival includes the parading of a fire mikoshi, a Taiko drum show, dancing, and fireworks. == Access == * Busses from: ** [[West Japan Railway Company]], [[Central Japan Railway Company]] [[Shingū Station]] on [[Kisei Main Line]] ** JR-West [[Kii-Tanabe Station]] blues ** [[Nanki–Shirahama Airport]] {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Kumano Hongu Taisha | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] |image = [[File:Inside the Kumano Hongu Taisha.jpg|270px]]
